strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem decomposition: the paper separates forgetting in MoE-based MCIT into router drift and expert drift, and supports each with a targeted diagnostic experiment (Fig. 1 routing-distribution snapshots; Fig. 1d router-retraining protocol) rather than only aggregate accuracy curves. This is a genuinely useful analysis contribution.

Main-paper results are reasonably comprehensive: benchmark comparison against seven recent baselines (Table 1), step-by-step component ablation (Table 2), direct verification that each component mitigates the drift it targets (Figs. 3-4), efficiency gains from adaptive activation (Fig. 5), and an interesting formatting-induced forgetting analysis (Figs. 6-7) that explains the non-monotonic drop-rebound pattern on ScienceQA.

The method has a coherent theoretical framing: Appendix A gives a bound justifying the null-space projection for preserving old routing, Appendix B derives the curvature-aware update as a Riemannian gradient under the historical input metric with the penalty absorbed into the learning-rate schedule, and Appendix C derives the AGOP-trace proxy for linear experts.
The method is rehearsal-free and the adaptive activation yields measurable training-time and memory savings, so the practical trade-offs are addressed rather than only accuracy.
weaknesses: Limited evaluation scope: experiments are confined to a single benchmark (CoIN, 8 tasks) with a single backbone (LLaVA-v1.5-7B). No second backbone, no other continual benchmarks (e.g., other task orders or longer sequences), and no variance across seeds or significance testing, so the reported ~2.8% gain over the strongest baseline is hard to assess for robustness.

Key hyperparameters are never specified: the energy threshold delta, damping constant mu, freezing threshold tau_score, and the number of retained components k are central to all three components, yet their values (and sensitivity analyses) are absent. This substantially weakens reproducibility, and no code release is mentioned.

Technical gaps in the covariance machinery: Eq. (3) updates the full covariance C^t, but the paper stores only the top-k principal components; how the subspace (V_parallel, V_perp) is maintained incrementally as new tasks arrive under truncated storage is not explained, and the extra memory/compute of per-layer covariance tracking (across all LLM blocks) is not accounted for in the efficiency analysis. There are also notation inconsistencies (k vs. r across Eq. 5 and Appendix A; alpha reused for both the covariance accumulator in Eq. 3 and the singular-value scalers in Eq. 7), and the sliding-window smoothing of singular values (Eq. 7) is introduced without motivation or ablation.

The constrained-optimization story in Appendix B is somewhat loose: coupling the dual variable lambda to the learning-rate schedule (Eq. 28) means the drift budget is not actually controlled at any explicit level, and the 'implicit absorption' of epsilon is a heuristic post-hoc justification rather than a demonstrated property of the realized updates.

The three components are individually well-known ideas (gradient projection onto null/input subspaces for continual learning, natural-gradient/K-FAC-style preconditioning, and expert freezing), so the contribution rests mainly on their combination and the diagnosis; the ablation in Table 2 also shows some components hurting specific tasks (e.g., activation reduces ScienceQA and TextVQA relative to w/ Expert, and w/ Expert alone outperforms the full method on TextVQA), which is not discussed.

Presentation issues: Figure 2 contains leftover placeholder/gibberish text ('draft draft draft', 'waWoooohhd'), and Table 1 shows SAME underperforming baselines on OCR-VQA and VQAv2 without discussion. The decision to freeze experts is updated inside the mini-batch loop (Algorithm 1), whose stability implications are unexamined.

strengths: The paper presents a clear, well-motivated decomposition of forgetting in MoE-based continual instruction tuning into router drift and expert drift, supported by a thoughtful diagnostic protocol (Fig. 1: snapshotting routers/experts, re-training the router on Task 1 to isolate expert drift). This diagnostic framing is genuinely informative and adds understanding beyond a new method.

The method has three reasonably distinct components (spectral-aware routing updates, curvature-aware/Riemannian preconditioning of expert updates, adaptive expert freezing), each with a concrete justification; the appendix derivations (null-space projection bound, penalty-method derivation of the Riemannian update, AGOP-trace proxy) are documented and mostly coherent.

The ablation is step-wise and shows each component contributes (50.58 -> 61.32 -> 65.89 -> 66.82), and the analysis sections (Figs. 3-5) tie each module to the specific failure mode it targets, which is more rigorous than typical MoE-continual-learning papers.

The formatting-induced forgetting analysis (Figs. 6-7) is an interesting empirical observation, and the baseline's non-monotonic ScienceQA drop-rebound pattern is well explained through case-mismatch error rates. The efficiency measurements for adaptive expert activation (Fig. 5) are a practical bonus.
weaknesses: Evidence is thin for a main-track claim of SOTA: all experiments use a single backbone (LLaVA-v1.5-7B) and a single benchmark (CoIN, 8 tasks). There is no second model scale, no task-order sensitivity analysis, no error bars or multiple seeds, and the margin over HiDe-LLaVA (+2.8%) is within plausible run-to-run variance for such evaluations.

There is a real technical inconsistency in the core spectral-aware routing design: Eq. (7) defines the scaling as alpha_i = 1/sigma_hat_i (larger scaling for smaller singular values), yet the accompanying text claims 'directions with smaller relative singular values ... are updated less aggressively.' These contradict each other, and the intended behavior is central to the router-drift mitigation claim. The related-material in Eq. (5) is also confusingly labeled (V_parallel described as 'important for the new task' while V_perp is described as old-task directions, whereas the null-space argument in Eq. (10)/Appendix A treats V_perp as near-zero-variance directions for all seen data).

Hyperparameter sensitivity is essentially unreported. The method introduces several critical knobs (energy threshold delta, damping mu, freezing threshold tau_score, sliding-window size, top-k principal components) but no sensitivity study, no ablation over them, and no default values stated in the main text. This significantly hurts reproducibility.

The ablation table reveals unexplained interactions: 'w/ Expert' outperforms the full method on TextVQA (66.85 vs 60.69), GQA (62.20 vs 61.70), and OCR-VQA, while 'w/ Router' alone already exceeds the full method on several tasks. The paper does not explain why adding the third component hurts some tasks, which weakens the claim of a cleanly composable design.

Presentation quality issues undermine confidence: Figure 2 (the overview figure) contains leftover placeholder/garbage text ('草稿草稿草稿', 'waWoooohhd'), the Related Work section is titled 'Relate Work,' and terminology is inconsistent (TextVQA vs 'TextQA'). These are signs of an insufficiently polished submission.

The computational claims are modest and partially redundant with existing continual-learning findings; the Riemannian preconditioning is closely related to well-known Fisher/K-FAC-style regularization (e.g., EWC-style covariance-based methods), and the paper does not adequately position the novelty relative to such prior work beyond a passing related-work paragraph. The comparison set, while broad, does not include a plain EWC/LwF-style MoE baseline to isolate whether the curvature machinery is needed.

No code release or reproducibility package is mentioned; given the many implementation-specific choices (per-layer projections, freezing schedules, sliding-window statistics), the method would be difficult to reproduce exactly from the manuscript alone.

strengths: The diagnostic analysis in Fig. 1 is a genuine strength: the paper cleanly disentangles router drift from expert drift using a re-routing protocol (retraining the router on Task 1 snapshots to remove misrouting as a confounder). This gives convincing empirical evidence that forgetting persists even under favorable routing, motivating the method rather than merely asserting the problem.

The three proposed components (spectral-aware routing in task-relevant subspaces, curvature-aware scaling derived from a soft-constrained functional-degradation objective, and utilization/importance-based expert freezing) are well-motivated, and the derivations in Appendices A-C are provided in reasonable detail, including a justified lightweight AGOP proxy for linear experts.
The benchmark evaluation on CoIN with LLaVA-v1.5-7B is reasonably broad (8 tasks, 7 baselines with public code), and SAME achieves the best average accuracy (66.82%) with consistent per-task gains.

The step-by-step ablation (Table 2) plus targeted analyses (Fig. 3 for routing stability, Fig. 4 for expert-level forgetting, Fig. 5 for efficiency, Fig. 6-7 for the interesting formatting-induced forgetting phenomenon) collectively support the claimed contributions of each module.

The adaptive expert activation yields measurable practical benefits (32.1 min average training-time reduction and 2.3K MiB/GPU memory reduction per task), which is a concrete efficiency contribution beyond accuracy alone.
The paper is generally well-written and clearly organized, with an honest limitations paragraph and an impact statement.
weaknesses: The evaluation is confined to a single benchmark (CoIN) and a single backbone (LLaVA-v1.5-7B). Generalization of the router-drift/expert-drift diagnosis and of SAME's benefits to other MLLMs (e.g., Qwen-VL, larger LLaVA variants) or other continual instruction-tuning sequences is not demonstrated, which limits the claimed significance.

Several theoretical arguments are looser than presented. In particular, the Appendix A 'null space' argument shows only that the projected energy of historical inputs is bounded by (1-δ) times total energy, which is not necessarily small in absolute terms unless δ is chosen very close to 1; the step to V⊥^T x^old ≈ 0 is hand-wavy. Similarly, the equivalence between the penalized objective and Riemannian gradient descent relies on first-order Taylor approximation and a particular coupling λ_t = 1/(2η_t) that is asserted rather than derived from first principles.

No variance estimates, multiple seeds, or statistical significance tests are reported for the main results, despite the aggregate margin over the strongest baseline being 2.8% and several per-task margins (e.g., GQA, OCR-VQA) being within ~1-2%.

The computational overhead of the method itself is incompletely characterized. Per-batch covariance updates, periodic SVDs of d×d matrices, and per-layer expert statistics all add cost; Fig. 5 reports savings from freezing experts but not the added overhead of spectral-aware routing and curvature-aware scaling relative to MoELoRA, making a fair end-to-end efficiency comparison difficult.

Sensitivity to key hyperparameters (energy threshold δ, damping μ, freezing threshold τ_score, drift budget ε/λ) is not analyzed, and no code release is mentioned, which weakens reproducibility of a method with this many moving parts.

The adaptive expert freezing uses signals (utilization and historical importance) that are themselves estimated under the evolving router; the paper does not analyze potential feedback effects (e.g., frozen experts reducing future utilization estimates and being frozen permanently), which could interact with router drift in unexamined ways.

The baseline ablation table (Table 2) starts from 'Baseline' = MoELoRA without constraint, but intermediate combinations (e.g., curvature-aware scaling without spectral-aware routing) are not reported, so component interactions cannot be fully assessed.

strengths: The paper offers a clear and well-motivated problem decomposition: diagnostic experiments (Fig. 1, Tab. 11) cleanly separate 'router drift' from 'expert drift', including an informative re-training protocol (freezing experts and re-training only the router) that isolates expert drift from misrouting.

The three components (spectral-aware routing updates, curvature-aware Riemannian preconditioning, adaptive expert freezing) are complementary and each is supported by targeted ablations (Tab. 4, Fig. 3, Fig. 4, Fig. 5), including design-choice ablations (Tab. 9) that compare against GPM-style hard projection and VPT-CPG-style scaling, showing the anisotropic scaling matters.

Evaluation is unusually thorough: three benchmarks including a new 10-task benchmark (TriGap) with heterogeneous domains and non-uniform data scales, three task orderings (Tab. 7-8), hyperparameter sensitivity (Tab. 6), forgetting metrics (Tab. 12), OOD transfer on MMMU (Tab. 13), and efficiency analyses (Tab. 14, Fig. 5).

The formatting-induced forgetting analysis (Fig. 6-7) is an interesting and concrete insight (drop-rebound cycles explained by letter-casing drift), and the appendix derivations (App. B-D) attempt to ground the update rules in null-space projection theory and Riemannian gradient descent.

Reproducibility infrastructure is reasonable: pseudocode, hyperparameter values, follow-up on benchmark construction details (Tab. 5, Fig. 9), and no obvious ethical concerns; limitations are honestly discussed.
weaknesses: The contribution is largely a combination of established ideas applied to MoE-LoRA continual tuning: null-space/gradient projection (GPM), curvature/Natural-Gradient-style preconditioning, and expert freezing. The novelty is incremental, and gains over the strongest recent baselines are modest (e.g., +2.87% over HiDe-LLaVA on CoIN, +2.08% over MoELoRA on TriGap), with regressions on some tasks (e.g., CLEVR on TriGap drops from 67.00 to 54.50; OCR-VQA slightly worse).

Table 2 (CoIN) adopts baseline results 'directly from their original publications' rather than reproducing them under the matched setup used for TriGap. Given differing training pipelines and evaluation protocols across papers, cross-paper comparability is questionable, and TriGap omits several strong baselines (SEFE, ProgLoRA, LLaVA-CMoE) that appear on CoIN.

Several theoretical elements are loose or have questionable validity: (i) the claim that V⊥X_old ≈ 0 (Eq. 10) holds only approximately since C^t includes new-task data and truncation is by energy threshold; (ii) the pseudo-inverse approximation (Eq. 15) applies 1/µ scaling in the orthogonal complement, whose effect relative to a plain identity scaling is not analyzed; (iii) the AGOP-trace argument (App. D) reduces to a routing-weighted average of ||x||², which discards directional information and weakens the 'curvature' framing; (iv) the hinge-penalty-to-Riemannian-gradient derivation relies on a first-order approximation and an implicit coupling of λ to the learning rate (Eq. 28) that is essentially a heuristic.

The adaptive expert activation mechanism has a circularity: utilization U(i) and importance F^cur(i) are updated from batches during the same task in which freezing decisions (Score(i) < τ_score) are made, and the timing/order of score computation, freezing, and covariance updates is not clearly specified, making exact reimplementation difficult.

Presentation flaws suggest a not-fully-polished manuscript: Figure 2 contains leftover draft text ('草稿草稿草稿', 'CR版本'); the phrase 'Under our surveillance' is odd; several very recent 2025/2026 citations (e.g., Prism arXiv:2605.26110, Roadside AAAI 2026) are hard to verify.

The sliding-window singular value scaling (Eq. 7-8, window over sorted singular values) appears heuristic; the justification that it makes the method robust to δ is asserted rather than analyzed, and the interaction between spectral routing scaling and curvature preconditioning (both derived from the same covariance C^t) is not disentangled beyond the component ablation.

strengths: The diagnostic motivation is a genuine strength: Fig. 1 cleanly separates router drift from expert drift via a re-training protocol (freeze experts, retrain only the router), and Appendix Tables 10-12 quantify each source of forgetting (e.g., router drift alone causes only ~1-2% drop, while total forgetting is much larger). This gives the paper an empirical story rather than a purely methodological one.

The formatting-induced forgetting analysis (Figs. 6-7) is insightful and novel: identifying that much of the 'drop-rebound' forgetting pattern on ScienceQA is letter-casing drift driven by the annotation conventions of subsequent tasks is a useful observation for the MCIT community.

The experimental scope is broad: three benchmarks (CoIN, UCIT, and the new TriGap with 10 heterogeneous tasks), task-ordering robustness (Appendix G), OOD evaluation on MMMU (Appendix K), efficiency analysis (Appendix L), and design-choice ablations (Appendix H, e.g., sliding-window vs. global scaling, adaptive vs. fixed-ratio freezing, GPM-style hard projection vs. anisotropic scaling).

TriGap is a reasonable addition as a benchmark: it deliberately uses datasets absent from LLaVA's training mixture, has non-uniform task scales (10k-40k), and longer sequences, addressing real gaps in CoIN/UCIT. Baselines were re-run under a unified setup on TriGap.

The method is rehearsal-free and memory-efficient in practice (low-rank covariance storage, ~0.5 MB/layer per Appendix L), and consistently improves final accuracy and average forgetting over strong baselines like HiDe-LLaVA and CL-MoE.
weaknesses: Presentation sloppiness undermines confidence: Figure 2 contains leftover draft placeholder text (the string '草稿草稿草稿 / CR版本' is visibly rendered inside the figure), and the bibliography contains numerous entries dated 2026 with implausible details (e.g., arXiv:2605.26110 and arXiv:2605.08839 are dated May 2026; 'Pico: Peer review in LLMs' at ICLR with page numbers 23100-23125). These citations are unverifiable at best and fabricated at worst, which is a serious trust issue for a submission.

The core 'spectral-aware routing' contribution is less substantive than claimed. Since V||V||^T + V_perp V_perp^T = I, Eq. (11) shows the combined update equals the raw gradient with only the near-identity scaling g(Σ) applied (α_i σ_i = σ_i/σ̂_i ≈ 1 for clustered singular values). The orthogonal-subspace narrative largely reduces to a mild anisotropic rescaling, and the claimed mechanism ('directions with smaller relative singular values updated less aggressively') rests on an ad hoc sliding-window heuristic with no theoretical grounding.

The theoretical justification in Appendix B is not rigorous: bounding E[||V_perp^T x_old||^2] ≤ (1-δ)Σσ_k^2 bounds only the tail energy relative to total energy, which can be large in absolute terms; the argument that uncentered covariance yields a near-null space for transformer hidden states is asserted rather than established. Similarly, Appendix C's 'rigorous derivation' relies on exact-penalty equivalence and a first-order Taylor approximation, and the coupling λ_t = 1/(2η_t) makes the drift budget ε implicitly time-varying, meaning the degradation constraint in Eq. (13) is never actually enforced.

The AGOP-based historical-importance proxy is very weak: for linear LoRA experts, tr(AGOP) = d_out·E[||x||^2] depends only on input norm, so F_cur(i) is merely routing-weighted input energy and carries no information about what the expert has learned. The 'historical importance' signal is therefore a crude heuristic, yet it is presented as a curvature-based sensitivity measure.

Comparison fairness is inconsistent: Table 2 (CoIN) results are 'directly adopted from their original publications' while TriGap results are reproduced under the authors' setup, mixing evaluation protocols; no seeds, variance, or significance testing is reported anywhere despite modest gains (+2.08% over MoE-LoRA on TriGap; per-task losses exist, e.g., FloodNetVQA 81.09 vs. MoE-LoRA's 90.41, CLEVR 54.50 vs. 67.00).

Originality is limited: the components are well-known continual-learning tools reassembled in a new setting — covariance-based subspace projection (GPM/OGD-style, acknowledged in Table 9), inverse-covariance gradient preconditioning (natural-gradient/K-FAC-like), and expert freezing (task-gating). The novelty lies mainly in the combination and the MCIT application, not in the techniques themselves.

The new-state claim that forgetting 'persists even under favorable routing' (Fig. 1d) is confounded: re-training the router on Task 1 with frozen later-stage experts still allows interference from representations upstream of the MoE layers, and the decreasing routing entropy reported as evidence of 'expert drift' has alternative explanations. The causal attribution between the two drift types is suggestive rather than established.

Several methodological details needed for reproduction are deferred or unclear: how often the covariance is recomputed/updated during a task (per batch, per Eq. 8-9 of Algorithm 1, involving an SVD per update?), the cost of this at every MoE layer, and whether V||/V_perp are shared or per-layer. Hyperparameter selection used only UCIT data, but sensitivity is only reported on UCIT, leaving transfer of δ, μ, τ_score to CoIN/TriGap unverified.

strengths: The paper identifies and cleanly separates two sources of forgetting in MoE-based MCIT (router drift vs. expert drift), supported by well-designed diagnostic experiments (Fig. 1: snapshotting routers/experts per task, re-training only the router to isolate expert drift; Tab. 11 isolating router-drift causality). This analysis is a genuine contribution and motivates the method well.

The proposed method is comprehensive: spectral-aware subspace routing with anisotropic singular-value scaling, curvature-aware (Riemannian-style) preconditioning of expert updates using historical input covariance, and adaptive task-level expert freezing. All components are rehearsal-free and the full training procedure is given in Algorithm 1.

Empirical coverage is extensive: three benchmarks (CoIN, UCIT, and the new 10-task TriGap with 250k+ instances), ablations of each component (Tab. 4), hyperparameter sensitivity (Tab. 6), task-ordering robustness (Tab. 7–8), quantitative forgetting analysis (Tab. 12), OOD generalization on MMMU (Tab. 13), and efficiency measurements (Tab. 14, Fig. 5).

The formatting-induced forgetting analysis (Figs. 6–7) is insightful — showing that much of the apparent 'drop-rebound' forgetting is driven by answer-casing convention drift rather than semantic forgetting — and this mechanistic finding strengthens the paper's empirical contribution.

The appendix derives the curvature-aware update from a constrained optimization view (hinge penalty → Lagrangian → Riemannian gradient) and provides design-choice ablations (Tab. 9) showing the anisotropic scaling beats GPM-style hard projection and constant subspace scaling.
weaknesses: A key theoretical claim is overstated. Appendix B argues V⊥ᵀx_old ≈ 0 because old-task inputs are 'part of the distribution used to construct C^t,' but the energy-threshold criterion bounds only the average energy over D≤t. A direction that is critical to an old task but low-energy in the mixed covariance would fall into V⊥, violating the claimed preservation (Eq. 10). The guarantee holds only in aggregate expectation, not per old-task direction, and no empirical verification of the bound is provided.

The AGOP-based historical importance proxy is weaker than presented: for a linear expert, tr(AGOP) reduces to d_out·E[||x||²] (Eq. 35), i.e., essentially routing-weighted input magnitude. This is a crude magnitude heuristic rather than a meaningful curvature/sensitivity signal, and no ablation against simpler proxies (e.g., raw routing frequency) is provided to justify the added framing.

Several elements feel heuristic or post-hoc: the sliding-window singular-value scaling (Eq. 7–8) is justified mainly by ablation; the coupling λ_t = 1/(2η_t) makes the tolerance ε vanish from the update rule, so the constrained-optimization derivation largely reduces to covariance preconditioning; and the combined router update ΔW∥ + ΔW⊥ (Eq. 11) has no analysis of their relative scaling.

Baseline comparability is inconsistent: on TriGap all baselines are re-run under the same setup, but CoIN (Tab. 2) results are 'directly adopted from their original publications,' which may use different backbones, epochs, and hyperparameters — weakening the claimed SOTA on the two standard benchmarks. Additionally, on TriGap SAME actually loses to MoE-LoRA on FloodNetVQA (81.09 vs 90.41) and CLEVR (54.50 vs 67.00), yet the text highlights 'FloodNet (81.09%)' as a strength without acknowledging the loss.

Presentation issues undermine polish: Figure 2 contains leftover drafting artifacts (the Chinese placeholder text '草稿草稿草稿 CR版本' inside the overview figure); the paper's central gains over the strongest baselines on CoIN/UCIT are moderate (e.g., +2.87 over HiDe-LLaVA on CoIN) and single-seed results with no variance reporting are given throughout.

The method carries several hyperparameters (δ, μ, τ_score, plus damping and freezing choices), and while sensitivity is studied on UCIT, the selection protocol (20% of UCIT data) may favor that benchmark; no code release is stated, which limits reproducibility of the multi-component pipeline. The new TriGap benchmark is a useful addition but its construction and evaluation protocol will need community validation.
